questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Excessive vitamin A intake (particularly as preformed retinol) during pregnancy is associated with which risk?

options.B: No known risk at any dose
options.C: Improved fetal bone mineralisation with no other effects
options.D: Reduced risk of neural tube defects

questions.explanation: Very high doses of preformed vitamin A during pregnancy are teratogenic and have been associated with congenital malformations, so intake should be carefully monitored.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Older adults are at particular risk of which vitamin deficiency due to reduced gastric acid secretion affecting its release from food?
questions.explanation: Reduced gastric acid production in many older adults impairs the release of protein-bound vitamin B12 from food, increasing the risk of deficiency.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which nutrient combination is particularly important in older adults to help maintain bone density and reduce fracture risk?
questions.explanation: Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake supports bone mineral density in older adults, helping to reduce the risk of osteoporotic fractures.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: The glycaemic index of a food is a measure of which of the following?

options.A: The vitamin and mineral density of a food
options.B: The total protein content of a food
options.C: The total calorie content of a food per 100 grams
options.D: How quickly a carbohydrate-containing food raises blood glucose levels compared with a reference food

questions.explanation: The glycaemic index ranks carbohydrate-containing foods by how rapidly and highly they raise blood glucose levels relative to a standard reference, such as glucose or white bread.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet emphasises which combination of dietary features?

options.A: High intake of red meat and full-fat dairy
options.B: High intake of refined sugar and processed foods
options.C: High intake of fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy, with reduced sodium
options.D: Complete elimination of all dietary fat

questions.explanation: The DASH diet emphasises fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while limiting sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars, and has been shown to lower blood pressure.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which micronutrient is commonly added to wheat flour in many countries specifically to reduce the risk of neural tube defects at a population level?
questions.explanation: Mandatory folic acid fortification of wheat flour has been implemented in many countries as a public health strategy to reduce the population-level incidence of neural tube defects.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a widely used field measurement for rapidly screening which condition in young children?
questions.explanation: MUAC is a simple, low-cost field measurement used to rapidly screen for acute malnutrition in children, particularly in resource-limited or emergency settings.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: A very low weight-for-height measurement in a child is used to identify which type of malnutrition?

options.D: Micronutrient deficiency only, with no calorie deficit

questions.explanation: Low weight-for-height reflects recent, acute weight loss or failure to gain weight appropriately, identifying wasting.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Dietary antioxidants such as vitamins C and E primarily function in the body by which mechanism?

options.B: Providing a direct source of dietary energy
options.C: Neutralising harmful free radicals and reducing oxidative cellular damage

questions.explanation: Antioxidants neutralise reactive free radicals, helping to reduce oxidative stress and associated cellular damage.

questions.subject: Nutrition
questions.question: Which term describes a nutrient that the body cannot synthesise in adequate amounts and must therefore obtain from the diet?
questions.explanation: An essential nutrient is one the body cannot produce in sufficient quantity itself and must be obtained through diet.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which symptom is most characteristic of iron-deficiency anaemia?
questions.explanation: Reduced haemoglobin concentration decreases oxygen delivery and commonly causes fatigue and exertional breathlessness.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which laboratory finding is most consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia with macrocytosis and an increased mean corpuscular volume.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which condition is a common cause of haemolytic anaemia?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency can cause episodic haemolysis, particularly following exposure to oxidative stress such as certain drugs or infections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which laboratory finding supports a diagnosis of haemolysis?
questions.explanation: Haemolysis commonly causes increased LDH and unconjugated bilirubin with reduced haptoglobin and an increased reticulocyte count.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which clinical feature is typical of sickle cell disease?

options.C: Persistent painless jaundice as the only feature
options.D: Increased platelet production as the defining feature

questions.explanation: Sickling of red cells can obstruct small blood vessels and produce recurrent painful vaso-occlusive episodes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which complication is particularly associated with sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation: Repeated splenic infarction can result in functional asplenia, increasing susceptibility to encapsulated bacterial infections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which clinical feature is characteristic of acute leukaemia?
questions.explanation: Bone-marrow replacement by leukaemic cells can impair normal red-cell, white-cell and platelet production, causing anaemia, infections and bleeding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which blood-count abnormality is particularly characteristic of aplastic anaemia?
questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia involves bone-marrow failure and commonly causes pancytopenia affecting red cells, white cells and platelets.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which clinical feature is typical of multiple myeloma?

options.C: Severe diarrhoea as the defining feature

questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma can cause lytic bone lesions and pain, recurrent infections, anaemia, renal impairment and hypercalcaemia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question: Which laboratory finding may occur in multiple myeloma?

options.B: Reduced immunoglobulin production in every patient

questions.explanation: Monoclonal immunoglobulin production can increase total serum protein and produce an abnormal paraprotein.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which artery supplies most of the face and scalp?
questions.explanation: The external carotid artery is a terminal branch of the common carotid artery and supplies many structures of the face and scalp. It ascends through the neck and gives branches including the facial and superficial temporal arteries. The common carotid artery pulse is more commonly palpated at the side of the neck, so the wording here identifies the external carotid by its branch relationship rather than by the usual pulse site.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for abduction of the arm from approximately 15 to 90 degrees?
questions.explanation: The deltoid muscle is the principal abductor of the arm from approximately 15 to 90 degrees. The supraspinatus initiates abduction during the first approximately 15 degrees, while further elevation above 90 degrees requires upward rotation of the scapula by muscles including the trapezius and serratus anterior.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which nerve is commonly referred to as the 'funny bone' nerve?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes superficially behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it can be compressed or struck against the bone. This commonly produces a tingling sensation radiating into the forearm and the little finger and medial half of the ring finger.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which chamber of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae?
questions.explanation: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from most of the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae. The blood then passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it through the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which bone forms the lateral prominence of the shoulder?
questions.explanation: The scapula forms the bony framework of the posterior shoulder. Its acromion, a lateral extension of the scapular spine, forms the palpable bony tip and roof of the shoulder and articulates with the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which muscle is the main extensor of the hip?
questions.explanation: The gluteus maximus is the main powerful extensor of the hip joint. It is especially active when rising from a seated position, climbing stairs, and running. It arises from the posterior ilium, sacrum, and coccyx and inserts mainly into the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: At approximately which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into the right and left common iliac arteries?
questions.explanation: The abdominal aorta typically bifurcates into the right and left common iliac arteries at approximately the level of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4). This is a standard anatomical landmark, although the exact level can vary slightly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which organ produces bile?
questions.explanation: The liver produces bile, which contains bile salts that help emulsify dietary fats and facilitate their digestion and absorption. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile before releasing it into the duodenum through the biliary ducts.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which structure connects bone to bone at a joint?
questions.explanation: A ligament is a band of dense connective tissue that connects bones to other bones. Ligaments help stabilize joints and guide or restrict movement. In contrast, tendons connect muscles to bones and transmit forces generated by muscle contraction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the arm?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve supplies the muscles of the posterior compartment of the arm, particularly the triceps brachii, which extends the elbow. It originates from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and travels through the radial groove of the humerus alongside the profunda brachii artery.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient prescribed combined oral contraceptives asks what happens if a dose is missed. Why is following the product-specific missed-pill advice important?

options.A: Missed doses prevent all ovulation for the next year
options.B: Missed doses can reduce contraceptive effectiveness
options.C: Missing one dose always causes infertility

questions.explanation: Missed hormonal contraceptive doses can reduce contraceptive protection, so product-specific instructions are important.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A woman receiving oxytocin during labour develops excessively frequent uterine contractions. What is the main concern?

options.C: Uterine hyperstimulation with possible fetal compromise

questions.explanation: Excessive oxytocin can cause uterine hyperstimulation, which may compromise uteroplacental blood flow and fetal wellbeing.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with postpartum haemorrhage receives oxytocin. What is the intended pharmacological effect?

options.B: Increase uterine contraction to help reduce bleeding

questions.explanation: Oxytocin stimulates uterine contraction and is used to help control postpartum haemorrhage.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with pre-eclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate and becomes markedly drowsy with reduced reflexes. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Ignore the finding because it is always expected
options.C: Assess for magnesium toxicity and follow the emergency treatment protocol

questions.explanation: Reduced reflexes and marked CNS depression can indicate magnesium toxicity and require prompt assessment and management.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with anaphylaxis develops hypotension, wheezing and facial swelling. Which medicine should be given promptly as first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line medicine for anaphylaxis because it rapidly treats airway, breathing and circulatory compromise.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient receiving adrenaline for anaphylaxis improves but remains under observation. Why is continued monitoring necessary?

options.A: Adrenaline prevents all future allergic reactions
options.C: The patient will inevitably develop renal failure
options.D: Biphasic reactions and recurrence of symptoms can occur

questions.explanation: Symptoms can recur after initial improvement, so continued observation is necessary following significant anaphylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient receiving heparin develops a significant fall in platelet count several days after treatment begins. What complication should be considered?
questions.explanation: A significant platelet fall during heparin therapy should raise concern for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, a potentially serious prothrombotic reaction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient taking warfarin is prescribed a new medicine that increases bleeding risk. What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.C: Ignore the interaction if the patient feels well
options.D: Review the interaction and monitor anticoagulation and bleeding risk

questions.explanation: Warfarin has important drug interactions, so the new medicine and anticoagulation status should be reviewed carefully.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient receiving a medicine that strongly induces hepatic drug-metabolising enzymes may require a higher dose of another medicine. Why?

options.B: The induced enzymes destroy all drugs in the stomach
options.C: Enzyme induction permanently blocks renal filtration
options.D: Enzyme induction can increase metabolism and reduce plasma concentrations of some drugs

questions.explanation: Enzyme induction can increase metabolism of susceptible medicines and reduce their plasma concentrations and effects.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient taking a medicine with a narrow therapeutic index develops toxicity after another medicine inhibits its metabolism. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: The interacting medicine has increased metabolism
options.B: Reduced metabolism has increased exposure to the narrow-therapeutic-index drug
options.C: The interacting medicine has increased clearance
options.D: The interacting medicine has reduced absorption only

questions.explanation: Enzyme inhibition can reduce metabolism, increasing drug exposure and the risk of toxicity, especially with narrow-therapeutic-index medicines.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: Which organism is a common bacterial cause of meningitis in young children?
questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an important bacterial cause of meningitis in children.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child has fever, headache and altered consciousness in an area where malaria is endemic. Which severe complication should be considered?
questions.explanation: Cerebral malaria can present with impaired consciousness and seizures and is a severe complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child develops fever followed by a widespread rash and Koplik spots are seen in the mouth. Which infection is most likely?
questions.explanation: Koplik spots and a characteristic febrile rash are strongly associated with measles.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child develops sudden pallor and bruising, and blood tests show pancytopenia. Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.explanation: Bone-marrow infiltration or failure in acute leukaemia can cause anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: Which feature is more suggestive of acute leukaemia than isolated iron-deficiency anaemia?
questions.explanation: Bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias suggest acute leukaemia rather than uncomplicated iron deficiency.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child has delayed passage of meconium and chronic constipation from early infancy. Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from absence of enteric ganglion cells and commonly presents with delayed meconium passage and constipation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden chest pain, fever and worsening breathlessness. Which complication should be suspected?
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome is a serious complication of sickle cell disease involving respiratory symptoms and a new pulmonary infiltrate.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of type 1 diabetes mellitus in children?
questions.explanation: Hyperglycaemia commonly causes polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss in children with type 1 diabetes.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes develops vomiting, abdominal pain and deep rapid breathing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis can cause vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul-type deep breathing due to metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.question: A child with fever, tachycardia and poor peripheral perfusion has delayed capillary refill. Which clinical condition should be considered?
questions.explanation: Poor perfusion with fever and cardiovascular instability may indicate septic shock.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which gas is a major indoor air pollutant associated with unvented biomass cooking stoves in developing nations?

options.B: Carbon monoxide and fine particulate matter (PM2.5)

questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion of solid fuels like wood or dung releases toxic carbon monoxide and particulate matter that cause severe respiratory illness.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: What is the primary function of the World Health Organization (WHO) International Health Regulations (IHR)?

options.A: To regulate domestic real estate transactions
options.B: To manage individual consumer credit scores
options.C: To set global corporate tax rates
options.D: To prevent, protect against, control, and provide a public health response to the international spread of disease

questions.explanation: The IHR is an international legal framework designed to assist countries in preventing and responding to acute public health risks that have the potential to cross borders.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which public health metric is calculated by dividing the number of maternal deaths due to pregnancy or childbirth complications by the total number of live births, multiplied by 100,000?
questions.explanation: The maternal mortality ratio tracks the risk of maternal death relative to the number of live births.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which intervention is most effective for preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV during pregnancy and delivery?

options.A: Complete cessation of breastfeeding without nutritional replacement
options.C: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for the mother and infant prophylaxis
options.D: Mandatory physical quarantine of the household

questions.explanation: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses maternal viral load and dramatically reduces transmission risk to the infant during pregnancy, labor, and breastfeeding.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which type of bias arises when study participants alter their natural behavior because they know they are being observed?
questions.explanation: The Hawthorne effect describes changes in individual behavior prompted by the awareness of being studied.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which environmental sanitation measure is most effective for preventing the spread of trachoma, a leading infectious cause of blindness?

options.C: Promoting facial cleanliness and regular face washing

questions.explanation: Trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis and spreads via eye-seeking flies and direct contact; facial cleanliness and hygiene break transmission.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: What is the primary public health purpose of administering high-dose vitamin A supplements to young children in endemic areas?

options.C: To prevent congenital neural tube defects
options.D: To reduce morbidity and mortality from measles and severe infectious illnesses

questions.explanation: Vitamin A supplementation strengthens immune function and significantly lowers severe illness and mortality risks in deficient children.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which population-level health metric combines years of life lost and years lived with disability into a single index?
questions.explanation: DALYs quantify total disease burden by capturing both premature mortality and non-fatal health losses.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which treatment train is essential for a safe municipal drinking water supply?

options.A: Proper coagulation, rapid sand filtration, and disinfection (chlorination)
options.C: Complete demineralization via reverse osmosis with added carbonation
options.D: Storage in open-air agricultural runoff reservoirs

questions.explanation: Standard water treatment plants utilize physical straining, filtration, and chemical disinfection to destroy enteric pathogens.

questions.subject: Community Health
questions.question: Which immunization strategy provides temporary, pre-formed immunity rather than stimulating the host's own immune response?

options.B: Administration of pre-formed human immunoglobulin antibodies

questions.explanation: Passive immunization introduces antibodies directly into the recipient, providing immediate but short-lived protection.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a bed alarm in fall prevention?

options.B: To alert staff when a patient attempts to exit the bed unassisted

questions.explanation: A bed alarm alerts staff when a patient at risk of falling attempts to leave the bed without assistance, allowing timely intervention.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: The 'Universal Protocol' in surgical settings primarily aims to prevent which type of error?
questions.explanation: The Universal Protocol, including a pre-procedure verification and a time-out, is designed to prevent wrong-site, wrong-procedure, and wrong-patient surgery.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: What does the acronym SBAR stand for in clinical communication?
questions.explanation: SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is a structured communication tool used to convey critical patient information clearly.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: Restraints in a healthcare setting should be used under which of the following conditions?

options.A: Only after less restrictive alternatives have failed and with a valid order
options.C: As a first-line intervention for confusion

questions.explanation: Restraints should be a last resort, applied only after less restrictive measures fail, with appropriate orders and regular reassessment.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: What is the primary goal of a 'time-out' performed immediately before a surgical procedure?

options.A: To confirm correct patient, procedure, and site with the whole team
options.D: To allow the surgical team a rest break

questions.explanation: The pre-procedure time-out is a final verification involving the whole team to confirm the correct patient, procedure, and surgical site.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: A nursing diagnosis such as 'Risk for Falls related to impaired mobility' is derived during which step of the nursing process?
questions.explanation: Formulating nursing diagnoses that identify actual or potential problems occurs during the diagnosis phase of the nursing process.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an expected outcome or goal statement in a nursing care plan?

options.A: To assign blame for poor outcomes
options.D: To provide a measurable standard for evaluating patient progress

questions.explanation: Expected outcomes provide specific, measurable criteria against which the patient's progress and the effectiveness of care can be evaluated.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: If an error is made in a paper medical record, what is the correct correction method?

options.A: Use correction fluid to cover the error
options.B: Tear out the page and rewrite it
options.C: Draw a single line through the error, initial, date, and write the correction

questions.explanation: Errors should be corrected with a single strike-through, initials, date, and the correct entry, preserving the original for legal accountability.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: Which of the following best describes an 'objective' assessment finding?

options.A: The patient reports pain as 7 out of 10
options.B: The nurse measures a blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg

questions.explanation: Objective data are measurable and observable findings, such as a directly measured blood pressure reading, rather than what the patient reports.

questions.subject: General Nursing
questions.question: Which statement best reflects the principle of confidentiality in nursing documentation?

options.B: Patient records may be discussed openly in public areas
options.C: All staff may access any patient's chart at any time
options.D: Access to patient information should be limited to those with a legitimate need to know

questions.explanation: Confidentiality requires that patient information be accessed only by those directly involved in care or with a legitimate professional need.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which drug is commonly used to treat Diphyllobothrium latum infection?
questions.explanation: Praziquantel is an effective treatment for Diphyllobothrium latum and other tapeworm infections.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: A 25-year-old male presenting with severe anal pruritus at night undergoes the transparent adhesive tape test, which reveals flattened, asymmetrical eggs containing a coiled embryo. What is this common nematode found worldwide and across African communities?
questions.explanation: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is a ubiquitous human pinworm diagnosed by applying adhesive tape to the perianal region to capture characteristic asymmetrical eggs deposited at night.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which stage of Plasmodium is injected into humans by an infected female Anopheles mosquito?
questions.explanation: During a blood meal, an infected female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites into the human bloodstream. They travel to the liver, where they invade liver cells and develop further.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which snail genus serves as the intermediate host for Schistosoma mansoni?
questions.explanation: Biomphalaria freshwater snails serve as the intermediate host in which Schistosoma mansoni larval stages develop before becoming infective cercariae.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'swimmer's itch,' a self-limiting dermatitis seen after exposure to contaminated water?

options.A: An allergic reaction to chlorine in swimming pools
options.B: A hypersensitivity reaction to cercariae of non-human (avian or animal) schistosomes penetrating human skin
options.C: A bacterial skin infection acquired from pool water
options.D: A fungal infection of the skin acquired from lake mud

questions.explanation: Swimmer's itch is caused by cercariae of bird or other animal schistosomes that penetrate human skin but cannot complete their life cycle, provoking a self-limiting hypersensitivity dermatitis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which drug is the treatment of choice for Trichomonas vaginalis infection?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole (or tinidazole) is the standard treatment for trichomoniasis in both partners.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Balantidium coli infection of the colon can cause a clinical picture resembling which other condition?
questions.explanation: Balantidium coli can invade the colonic mucosa and cause flask-shaped ulcers and dysentery similar in presentation to amoebic dysentery.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which serological technique, using fluorescently labelled antibodies, is commonly used to detect antibodies against parasites such as Toxoplasma and Leishmania?
questions.explanation: The indirect fluorescent antibody test uses fluorescently labelled secondary antibodies to detect patient antibodies bound to parasite antigen on a slide, aiding serological diagnosis.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which domestic animal serves as the definitive host for Echinococcus granulosus, harbouring the adult tapeworm?
questions.explanation: Dogs and other canids serve as the definitive host, carrying the small adult tapeworm in their intestines and shedding eggs in their faeces.

questions.subject: Parasitology
questions.question: Which intestinal protozoan parasite is transmitted through fecally contaminated water and causes watery diarrhea, particularly in travelers returning from endemic areas?
questions.explanation: Cyclospora cayetanensis is a coccidian protozoan acquired via contaminated water or produce, causing prolonged watery diarrhea and gastrointestinal distress.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has a substantial reduction in arterial oxygen content despite normal alveolar ventilation. Which change could produce this finding?
questions.explanation: Reduced haemoglobin concentration lowers arterial oxygen content even when oxygen loading by the lungs is normal.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient develops severe metabolic acidosis. Which change would occur as part of the body's immediate respiratory compensation?
questions.explanation: Increased ventilation removes carbon dioxide, reducing hydrogen ion concentration and helping compensate for metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has a marked increase in plasma osmolarity after inadequate water intake. Which physiological response occurs to help restore osmotic balance?

options.A: Increased ADH secretion and increased water reabsorption
options.D: Reduced ADH secretion and increased urine volume

questions.explanation: Increased plasma osmolarity stimulates ADH secretion and thirst, promoting water conservation and intake.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has reduced sympathetic activity during rest. Which cardiovascular effect would be expected compared with a state of increased sympathetic activity?

options.B: Reduced heart rate and vascular tone
options.D: Increased heart rate and vascular resistance

questions.explanation: Reduced sympathetic activity decreases stimulation of the heart and many vascular beds, contributing to lower heart rate and vascular tone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has reduced plasma albumin but normal capillary hydrostatic pressure. Why is peripheral oedema more likely to develop?

options.A: Increased albumin causes excessive water retention
options.B: Reduced blood volume prevents all filtration
options.C: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure favours filtration
options.D: Increased plasma oncotic pressure prevents reabsorption

questions.explanation: Lower plasma albumin reduces the inward osmotic force that normally helps retain fluid within capillaries, favouring net filtration into tissues.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has a decrease in renal perfusion but the reduction remains within the kidney's autoregulatory range. What is the primary purpose of renal autoregulation?

options.A: To maintain relatively stable renal blood flow and GFR
options.B: To increase urine production regardless of blood pressure
options.C: To prevent all changes in renal blood flow

questions.explanation: Renal autoregulation helps maintain relatively stable renal blood flow and GFR despite moderate changes in arterial pressure.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has impaired movement of the diaphragm because of respiratory muscle weakness. What immediate effect would this have on ventilation?
questions.explanation: Reduced diaphragmatic movement decreases the change in thoracic volume during inspiration, reducing tidal volume.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient has a significant reduction in circulating blood volume. Which combination of renal and hormonal responses would help conserve fluid?

options.A: Reduced sympathetic activity and increased natriuresis
options.C: Reduced ADH and increased sodium excretion
options.D: Increased urine formation and reduced renin

questions.explanation: Reduced circulating volume activates mechanisms including ADH release and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, promoting water and sodium conservation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: A patient develops severe hypocalcaemia. Which physiological effect helps explain the development of muscle spasms and increased neuromuscular excitability?

options.A: Higher extracellular calcium blocks all action potentials
options.B: Lower extracellular calcium increases membrane excitability
options.C: Hypocalcaemia causes immediate muscle paralysis in all cases
options.D: Lower calcium prevents neurotransmitter release completely

questions.explanation: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for excitation of nerve and muscle membranes, increasing neuromuscular excitability.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.question: Which factor is primarily responsible for the movement of water across a selectively permeable cell membrane during osmosis?
questions.explanation: Water moves across a selectively permeable membrane in response to differences in effective solute concentration.
